title: The Educated Barbarian: Hagakure analysis (part. 13)
summary: NH announces the next reading cycle on stoicism, then works through the start of Hagakure book two: enduring hardship, the warrior values of wisdom, compassion and courage, single-minded purpose, prevention over cure, self-belief and lifelong learning. He ties the passages to discipline, training one day at a time and health.
claims: Next reading cycle is stoicism: a Stoic Classics collection (Marcus Aurelius' Meditations, Epictetus' Enchiridion, Seneca's On the Happy Life) first, then Epictetus' Discourses as the core text
Men who never endured hardship lack resilience at their core; adversity is best met while young
People handed a little power for the first time often abuse it immediately because they were never acclimated to it
Do not dodge difficulties: every hardship prepares you for the next, and a weak man cannot even help the people he loves
Bushido's core values are wisdom, compassion and courage; courage comes last and two of the three are expressed through the spirit, making bushido mainly a spiritual teaching
You get wiser simply by listening, to people and to nature; know one thing deeply and you know ten thousand things
Compassion should be given freely, minimizing self-gratification and expecting nothing in return
Courage is not an action but the absence of fleeing or renouncing: simply stand your ground and endure
Being dishonest with yourself slowly erodes your strength of will; stay truthful even if it creates friction, while using tact with sensitive people
He says he has not been sick in 10 years
Prevention beats cure: build a body so strong illness cannot touch it instead of relying on drugs after getting sick
Hard work is realized one step at a time: 100 days of training is daunting but you can always endure one day, like moving a mountain one rock at a time
Will is applied to one thing at a time; single-minded focus on the present task lets you accomplish anything
The greatest gift to a child is making them realize the power of hard work; once learned it is never unlearned
Nostalgia for the good old days is futile and black-pilling is unproductive; adapt, improve the present and fight the darkness you see
Both those who live in the past and those who despise all tradition are misguided; the progressive camp is more dangerous because it pushes change too fast
A pure mind keeps its values unbent by the outside world; corruption of the soul spreads to the spirit and then the body
Telling yourself you are the best is self-belief, not arrogance; everything that happens physically happens first spiritually
Chasing perfection, which does not exist, dissolves limitations, since limitations are only what stands between you and perfection
Most modern people inflict more harm than good on their bodies through food and habits; body and spirit have been divorced
Doctors rarely push prevention partly because many do not practice it themselves and every profession tends to perpetuate its own need
Strong-minded people find difficulties exciting, something to defeat, while weak ones feel they are drowning
Anecdote: cows in his family's mountains keep big horns because wolves remain, yet never attack walkers; likewise a wasp has no reason to sting you
Do not build anxiety about threats with no clear sign; prevent what you know is coming and ignore what you cannot foresee
Everyone would be happier with a purpose; if you have none, your purpose is to find one
Accepting that life will end gives existence its flavor; at 25 he finds it easy to be brave and hopes to keep that spirit as he ages
The way is endless and achieved only at death; a man who stops learning or accepting challenges is already dead
